Alfred Delp S.J. — (1907–1945). See A. Delp, Gesammelte Schriften, vol. 4, Frankfurt am Main 1985, p. 312.

Schmitt uses the expression in his 1945 legal opinion on aggressive war to describe Nazi crimes. See Angriffskrieg, p. 16, and editor Quaritsch’s note on pp. 86 ff. concerning the origin of the phrase.

Edmund A[loysius] Walsh — The American Jesuit and geoscientist Edmund A. Walsh (1885–1956) worked with the American chief prosecutor at the Nuremberg war-crimes trials and questioned the geographer Karl Haushofer. Walsh regarded Schmitt’s theory of large territorial spaces as the legal counterpart to Haushofer’s geopolitical theory.
On pp. 12–13 of the book mentioned by Schmitt, Walsh writes:

“Unfortunately, the purely geographical content of this false geopolitics was supplemented by a parallel rationalization in the field of law and legal science […] Legality became a geographical concept and, worse still, we saw the caricature of jurisprudence popularized by Karl Schmitt of the University of Berlin.”

“poor Gurian” — Waldemar Gurian (1902–1954), political scientist. During the 1920s he was on friendly terms with Schmitt in Bonn. After emigrating in 1933, however, he became one of Schmitt’s most dangerous opponents.

Gurian is often credited with coining the influential description of Schmitt as the “crown jurist of the Third Reich.” In fact, Kurt Hiller had already written in Die Weltbühne on 4 October 1932, p. 499:
“This social-revolutionary nationalist [Karl O. Paetel] appeals to the conservative Catholic constitutional lawyer Carl Schmitt, the crown jurist of the Papen dictatorship …”
On Hiller, see also below, note to p. 167.

On Gurian, see his correspondence with Schmitt in Schmittiana NF I, 2011, pp. 59–111; also BW Mohler, p. 95; and Ellen Thümmler, Katholischer Publizist und amerikanischer Politikwissenschaftler. Eine intellektuelle Biografie Waldemar Gurians, Baden-Baden 2011.
“The boundary has something magical about it,” says Kassner — Rudolf Kassner, Sämtliche Werke, vol. 9, Pfullingen 1990, p. 490.
Hic jacet — “Here lies,” shortened from the common gravestone inscription:
Hic iacet pulvis, cinis et nihil.
“Here lie dust, ashes, and nothing else.”

“Whether actions are good or evil is judged by their outcome (§ 4). But since it is very easy to go wrong in such judgments if one does not consider all the particular circumstances under which an action takes place, especially if one relies too heavily on the expectation that similar cases will turn out in the same way (§ 331, Met.), it happens very often that the outcome declares evil what we had thought good, and good what had seemed evil to us.”
Christian Wolff, Vernünfftige Gedanken von der Menschen Thun und Lassen, Frankfurt/Leipzig 1736, pp. 60–61.
on Nebel’s Tyranny and Freedom — Gerhard Nebel, Tyrannis und Freiheit, Düsseldorf 1947.
Goethe’s heroic poem on old Blücher — Goethe, Dem Fürsten Blücher von Wahlstadt die Seinen:
“In waiting and in war, In fall and victory, Conscious and great! So he tore us free From our enemies.”
Goethes Werke, vol. 1, Hamburg edition, p. 345.
Cochin — Augustin Cochin (1876–1916), historian of the French Revolution, which he studied from a sociological perspective.
Schmitt owned A. Cochin, Les sociétés de pensée et la démocratie. Études d’histoire révolutionnaire, 6th ed., Paris 1921, RW 579 no. 1158. He had already referred to it in 1936; see PuB, p. 262.
Bryce — James Bryce (1838–1922), British jurist, historian, and politician.
Ostrogorski — Moisei Yakovlevich Ostrogorski (1854–1921), Russian political scientist and scholar of political parties.
Roberto Michels — Robert or Roberto Michels (1876–1936), German-Italian sociologist and major theorist of political parties. Schmitt may have met him through Max Weber.
Michels first appears in Schmitt’s diary at the beginning of 1923; see Tb 1921–24, p. 159.
ces êtres inhumains … — See A. Cochin, Les sociétés de pensée, chapter 10, “Le dilemme.”

Villiers de l’Isle-Adam — Auguste de Villiers de l’Isle-Adam (1838–1889), French writer and one of the founders of French Symbolism. His novel L’Ève future, critical of modern science, made a powerful impression on Schmitt. See Tb 1921–24.

the Chief Forester — A cunning yet outwardly respectable figure created by Ernst Jünger, first emerging from dreams during “a stormy night in the Harz” in 1934. The figure later appeared in the second version of The Adventurous Heart and in the story On the Marble Cliffs.
The Chief Forester has been identified with several historical figures, including Hitler and Göring.
In March 1940 Schmitt wrote to Jünger:

“On Easter Monday we were invited to the home of the Yugoslav envoy here, Andrić, who proved to be a remarkable reader and connoisseur of your book On the Marble Cliffs, far beyond the usual readers who treat it as a roman à clef. I normally shock the latter by claiming that the Chief Forester is Prince Bismarck.”
BW EJ, pp. 88–89. See also above, note to p. 15.
Le Convive des dernières fêtes — Title of a story by Villiers de l’Isle-Adam. Schmitt first read it on 12 March 1923; see Tb 1921–24, p. 169.
“a helot who swallowed with grinding teeth …” — From the poem “Am 25. Sonntage nach Pfingsten” by Annette von Droste-Hülshoff.
Nordic Society in the Böttchergasse — The Nordic Society, founded in 1921 and placed in the service of National Socialism after 1933, had its headquarters in Breite Straße in Lübeck.
Schmitt probably means the “Nordic Thing,” which began meeting in Bremen’s Böttcherstraße in 1933 at the initiative of the businessman Ludwig Roselius.
Gobineau — Arthur de Gobineau (1816–1882), French writer, diplomat, and racial theorist.
Schmitt is referring to the following edition: Arthur de Gobineau, Essai sur l’inégalité des races humaines, vols. 1–2, Paris 1884. Schmitt’s copy survives among his papers, RW 265 no. 27029.
Martin Beheim-Schwarzbach — Schmitt probably means his story “Vom leibhaftigen Schmerz,” published in 1946.
discussion with Sartre — Sartre came to Berlin for a production of his play The Flies.

On 1 February 1948 a much-discussed and highly contentious debate took place at the Hebbel Theater, with representatives from the Soviet Union also taking part. Sartre defended an ethics of unlimited freedom and responsibility.
The production and debate are generally regarded as the beginning of the German reception of Sartre.
A transcript of the discussion appeared in Verger. Revue du spectacle et des lettres pour la Zone Française d’Occupation 1, no. 5, 1948, pp. 109–123. See also Der Spiegel, 7 February 1948.
Steiniger — Peter Alfons Steiniger (1904–1980), professor of international law at Humboldt University in East Berlin. Hans Peters had qualified him as a lecturer in 1947.
Steiniger took part in the discussion with Sartre.
He had studied under Carl Schmitt in Bonn and was already politically active as a communist at the time, including as a contributor to Die Weltbühne.

His dissertation, supervised by Albert Hensel—Die Fragen der Provinzialreform in Preußen; Schmitt’s copy survives as RWN 0260 no. 215—was rejected in 1926 by the second examiner, Erich Kaufmann, probably for political reasons. Schmitt was then asked to give his own assessment.
Schmitt also rejected the dissertation, but credited Steiniger with great talent and intellectual sharpness and recommended that he revise it.
Steiniger submitted a new dissertation in 1928, which Hensel and Schmitt both graded rite.
Among Schmitt’s papers are four handwritten pages by Steiniger from 1926, “Anmerkungen zum Thema: Demokratie u. Parlamentarismus,” inspired by Schmitt’s work on parliamentarism, RW 265 no. 20041.
From 1928 Steiniger worked at the Berlin School of Commerce and continued to have personal contact with Schmitt.
During the Nazi period Steiniger, who was Jewish and remained in Germany, was in danger. Under the pseudonym Peter A. Steinhoff he published novels, one of which was titled Der Schatten Gottes.
In the early GDR, Steiniger became the leading scholar of international law.

See Kristin Kleibert, Die Juristische Fakultät der Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin im Umbruch. Die Jahre 1948 bis 1951, Berlin 2010; M. Stolleis, Geschichte des öffentlichen Rechts in Deutschland, vol. 4, Munich 2012, pp. 107–108 and passim.
libertas libertate perit — The complete passage reads:
Libertas inquit populi quem regna coercent, Libertate perit.
“The freedom of a people held down by tyranny, he says, is destroyed by freedom itself.”
Ilya Ehrenburg — (1891–1967), Russian writer and journalist, known for his wartime propaganda articles against Germany.
Pauca tamen suberunt priscae vestigia fraudis — “A few traces of the old guilt will nevertheless remain.” Virgil, Fourth Eclogue.
Erunt etiam altera bella — “There will also be new wars.” Ibid.
plena securitas in hac vita non expectanda — “Complete security is not to be expected in this life.”
The idea goes back to Augustine. “Peace and security” was also a slogan associated with the Antichrist; see 1 Thessalonians 5:3.

“And so we fight against the enemies …” — From the Moravian Daily Texts, which Margarete Oberheid sent Schmitt every year and which he read regularly. Surviving copies are preserved among his papers, RW 265 nos. 20966 and 20967.
“More’s gay genius” — From William Wordsworth’s poem “Apology,” in Poetical Works, edited by Henry Reed, Philadelphia and elsewhere, 1837, p. 301:

Lightly for both the bosom’s lord did sit Upon his throne; unsoftened, undismayed By aught that mingled with the tragic scene Of pity or fear; and More’s gay genius played With the inoffensive sword of native wit, Than the bare axe more luminous and keen.
Christoph Steding’s “non-book” — C. Steding, Das Reich und die Krankheit der europäischen Kultur, Hamburg 1939.
See Schmitt’s review in PuB, pp. 309–334.

Steding (1903–1938), a historian strongly influenced by Max Weber, occupied a somewhat unusual position within Nazi scholarship. See Helmut Heiber, Walter Frank und sein Reichsinstitut für Geschichte des neuen Deutschland, Stuttgart 1966.
my lecture in Barcelona in October 1929 — C. Schmitt, “Die europäische Kultur im Zwischenstadium der Neutralisierung,” in Europäische Revue 5, 1929, pp. 517–530.
A revised version was later published under the title “Das Zeitalter der Neutralisierungen und Entpolitisierungen,” in BdP, pp. 66–81.
“That is the feeling of the unchangeable …” — See Tb 1912–15, p. 169.
“They can afford to do that” — Ibid., p. 106.
The “Privy Councillor” is Hugo am Zehnhoff.
Pepys — Samuel Pepys (1633–1703), author of an extensive diary often regarded as an early document of narcissistic subjectivism.

“The Temptation of Francisco de Vitoria” — Alfred Verdross-Drossberg, “Die internationale Anerkennung der Menschenrechte – Die Versuchung des Franciscus Vitoria,” in Wort und Tat 1, no. 3, October 1946, pp. 7 ff.
“the accident of my own present …” — See below, note to p. 260.
ξίφος ἐν μύρτου κλαδί — “The sword in the myrtle branch.”
From an epigram by the Greek poet Simonides, 557/556–468/467 BC.
See Annette Rink, Das Schwert im Myrtenzweige. Antikenrezeption bei Carl Schmitt, Vienna/Leipzig 2000, p. 24, note 49.
Gustav Würtenberg — G. Würtenberg, Nero oder die Macht der Dämonen, Düsseldorf 1948.
the book by L. Klages on Alfred Schuler — Ludwig Klages (1872–1956), philosopher of life, psychologist of expression, and graphologist.
Schmitt means A. Schuler, Fragmente und Vorträge aus dem Nachlaß, with an introduction by Ludwig Klages, Leipzig 1940.
